screens.title: Cross-Program Invocation (CPI)
screens.narratorSegment: Cross-Program Invocation, or CPI, is the mechanism Solana uses to let one deployed program request work from another program. CPI enables composability: your program can rely on a shared token program for transfers, or call a lending program to update state, rather than reimplementing that logic. In practice CPI means assembling the exact instruction the callee expects, collecting the required AccountInfo objects in the correct order, and deciding whether the calling program must supply a signature. That decision determines whether you use invoke or invoke_signed. A concrete example you will see in this chapter is an escrow program delegating an SPL Token transfer. The escrow does not implement token logic; it calls the SPL Token Program and, if the escrow owns the source account, it uses invoke_signed and signer seeds so the program can sign for a Program Derived Address. We will also cover defensive practices: verifying ownership, writable flags, and signer expectations, and how misordered accounts commonly cause runtime failures. By the end of this chapter you will be able to assemble CPI calls, choose the appropriate invoke function, supply signer seeds for PDAs, and validate accounts before making external calls. Consider: what checks would you perform first before handing an external program access to your accounts?

screens.title: What is Cross-Program Invocation (CPI)?
screens.narratorSegment: Cross-Program Invocation is the mechanism that lets one Solana program ask another deployed program to execute an instruction on its behalf. Put simply, CPI turns programs into modular services: instead of reimplementing token transfer logic you call the SPL Token Program. A clear definition helps you reason about authority, ownership, and the limits of each program's control. The callee receives a prepared instruction and an ordered slice of AccountInfo objects describing which accounts to read or modify, and it enforces its own validation rules. A useful mental model is: the invoker composes an instruction packet and offers it to a callee that already knows how to act on those accounts. A concrete example is an escrow program that needs to transfer tokens: the escrow builds the token transfer instruction that the SPL Token Program understands, supplies the source account, destination account, authority account, and token program account, and calls invoke_signed if the escrow must sign via a PDA. A common misconception is thinking CPI magically shares signer authority; it does not. The invoking program only gains signing power for a derived PDA when it supplies correct signer seeds to invoke_signed. As you learn CPI, keep that model in mind: instruction packet, account ordering, and explicit signing are the three pillars.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is CPI?
Definition

CPI allows one program to call another program's instruction with a specific set of accounts and optional signer seeds.

Metaphor
Think of the invoker as a client sending a request packet to a service that already knows how to perform the operation.
Key Takeaway

CPI is explicit: you must assemble instruction data, ordered accounts, and provide signer seeds when a PDA should sign.

Concrete Example: Escrow token transfer
  • Invoker constructs an SPL Token transfer instruction with amount and authority fields.
  • Invoker collects AccountInfo objects: source, destination, authority, token program in the expected order.
  • If the authority is a PDA the program controls, it calls invoke_signed and supplies signer seeds to sign on behalf of that PDA.
Common misconception
CPI does not implicitly grant signing power; invoke_signed is required for PDAs and signing must be explicit via seeds.
Check
Always confirm the callee's expected account order before calling.

screens.title: AccountInfo and how accounts are passed
screens.narratorSegment: In Solana, accounts are described to the callee as a slice of AccountInfo objects. Each AccountInfo contains metadata: the public key, the owner program, whether the account signed the original transaction, whether it is writable, and a pointer to its data. When you prepare a CPI you must assemble each AccountInfo the callee expects and pass them in the exact order the callee's instruction parser assumes. Practically, that means you cannot rely on position-agnostic lookup — the callee binds roles to positions: account 0 might be the source token account, account 1 the destination, account 2 the authority, and so on. A concrete scenario is the SPL Token transfer instruction: it expects source, destination, authority (and the token program account in some cases). If you swap those positions the SPL Token Program will read the wrong account as the authority and the instruction will fail validation. Another important detail is the distinction between account. owner and program-derived ownership: you must verify that an account that must be owned by a particular program actually is, and that a PDA you expect to sign is derived from your program id and known seeds. A common rookie error is trusting the client-supplied accounts without checking owner and signer flags. Always perform those checks before constructing and issuing a CPI.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › AccountInfo and Passing
AccountInfo essentials
  • Each AccountInfo provides key, owner, is_signer, is_writable, and data pointer.
  • The callee expects accounts in a strict positional order; mismatch causes failures.
  • Verify account.owner matches expected program and that signer/writable flags meet requirements.
Example role mapping
For an SPL Token transfer the expected order commonly includes source, destination, authority, and token program. Follow callee docs exactly.
Common mistake

Passing accounts in the wrong order or forgetting to check owner leads to invalid account errors in the callee.

Annotated account list
source_token_account — must be an SPL token account and writable.
destination_token_account — owner should be token program; typically writable.
authority_account — must match expected signer or PDA derived from program id.
token_program — must equal the SPL token program id.
Key Takeaway

Account position and metadata drive how the callee behaves; validate them before CPI.

screens.title: invoke vs invoke_signed
screens.narratorSegment: Solana exposes two primary runtime helpers for CPI: invoke and invoke_signed. invoke is used when the invoking program does not need to sign for any accounts in the callee instruction. In such cases the required signatures are already present on the transaction, usually because the end user signed, and the invoker simply relays the instruction. A concrete example is a proxy program that forwards a user-signed delegation instruction to the SPL Token Program. invoke_signed is required when the invoking program must sign for a Program Derived Address it controls. With invoke_signed you supply signer seeds: byte arrays used by the runtime to reconstruct the PDA and allow the program to sign on its behalf. This enables common patterns like a program-owned escrow or a wrapper program that mints tokens where the mint authority is a PDA. A frequent misconception is believing that invoke_signed automatically signs any account; it only signs PDAs derived from your program id using the seeds you supply. Also be aware that the signer seeds must exactly reconstruct the PDA and that all PDA signer accounts passed to the callee must be in the expected positions. The practical rule is: if any account in the callee instruction requires a signature that your program must provide, use invoke_signed with the correct seeds; otherwise invoke suffices.

keyIdea.title: Choose invoke carefully
keyIdea.text: Use invoke when no program signature is needed; use invoke_signed when the program must sign for PDAs using exact signer seeds.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › invoke vs invoke_signed
invoke

Use when all required signatures are already present and your program does not need to sign for any accounts.

Example use
A proxy that forwards a user-signed instruction to the SPL Token Program without adding signatures.
invoke_signed

Use when your program must sign on behalf of a PDA it controls by supplying signer seeds to reconstruct the PDA for the runtime.

Example use
An escrow program transferring tokens from a PDA-owned token account where the program must provide the PDA signature.

screens.title: Program Derived Addresses and signer seeds
screens.narratorSegment: Program Derived Addresses, or PDAs, are public keys derived deterministically from seeds and a program id. They allow a program to have accounts it effectively controls without a private key. To use a PDA as a signer during CPI, you must call invoke_signed with the exact set of seeds used to derive that PDA. The runtime reconstructs the PDA from seeds and program id, verifies the PDA, and if it matches the supplied account the runtime treats it as signed by the program. A practical pattern: when a program owns a token account, that account is often owned by the program via a PDA authority. To transfer from that account you must supply the PDA as the authority and call invoke_signed with the original seeds. A common pitfall is using seeds that do not exactly match the derivation: even a single byte difference prevents the runtime from recognizing the PDA and the callee will reject the missing signature. Another mistake is forgetting to include the PDA account in the AccountInfo slice passed to the callee or placing it in the wrong position. When designing seeds, choose stable domain-like seeds such as a descriptive string plus a bump. Document the seeds, use a deterministic bump, and always check the PDA owner before relying on it as an authority.

keyIdea.title: Seeds create PDA signers
keyIdea.text: Signer seeds reconstruct a PDA for the runtime so your program can sign for program-owned accounts using invoke_signed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › PDAs & Seeds
What are PDAs?

Deterministic public keys derived from seeds and a program id. They have no private key and are signed for by the runtime when supplied with matching seeds.

Design tip
Use expressive seeds like a domain string and a bump so the PDA purpose is obvious and stable.
Common mistakes
  • Using the wrong seeds or bump so the PDA cannot be reconstructed.
  • Omitting the PDA account from the AccountInfo slice or placing it in the wrong order.
Key Takeaway

If your program must sign, design reliable seeds and always pass the PDA where the callee expects it.

screens.title: Escrow token transfer using invoke_signed
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concise token transfer pattern where a program-owned PDA signs an SPL Token transfer using invoke_signed. The invoker prepares the SPL Token transfer instruction with the source token account, destination token account, and authority set to the PDA. It then constructs the AccountInfo slice in the exact order the SPL Token Program expects. Next, the program provides signer seeds that reconstruct the PDA, wrapped as an array of seed slices, and calls invoke_signed. In practice you should first validate that the token program account matches the SPL Token Program ID, that the source and destination are proper token accounts owned by the token program, and that the PDA is derived from your program id using the expected seeds. A misconception to avoid is trusting the provided authority account without derivation checks; instead compute the expected PDA locally and compare the public key. For a concrete example, the escrow pattern passes source, destination, pda_authority, and token_program in that order and uses a seeds array such as [b"escrow", bump]. After invoke_signed completes, check the result and update any on-chain escrow state. As a closing question: how would you structure your checks so that no external call happens until all invariants are validated?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Escrow transfer
Step summary
  1. Validate token program id and that accounts are token accounts.
  2. Confirm PDA derivation and ownership of the source token account.
  3. Create transfer instruction for SPL Token Program and collect AccountInfos in expected order.
  4. Call invoke_signed with signer seeds and handle the result.
Analogy
Think of seeds as the program's sealed stamp; only with the right stamp will the runtime treat the PDA as signed.
// Example excerpt: building transfer instruction and calling invoke_signed
let transfer_instruction = token_instruction::transfer(
  token_program.key,
  source_token_account.key,
  destination_token_account.key,
  pda_authority.key,
  &[],
  amount,
)?;

let pda_seeds = &[b"escrow", &[bump]];
let signer_seeds = &[&pda_seeds[..]];

invoke_signed(
  &transfer_instruction,
  &[
    source_token_account.clone(),
    destination_token_account.clone(),
    pda_authority.clone(),
    token_program.clone(),
  ],
  signer_seeds,
)?;
Key Takeaway

Assemble instruction and accounts correctly; provide exact signer seeds so runtime recognizes the PDA signer.

Common Mistake

Not checking token program id or passing accounts in the wrong order causes runtime errors.

screens.title: Implementing a Simple Token Wrapper (starter code)
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on starter demonstrates the wrapper program pattern: your program will call the SPL Token Program's mint_to instruction using invoke_signed so a PDA acts as mint authority. The starter structure provides a process_instruction entrypoint that expects accounts for the token mint, destination token account, PDA mint authority, and the token program account. Your task is to define the PDA seeds, construct the mint_to instruction passing the PDA as authority, prepare the AccountInfo slice in the order the SPL Token Program expects, and call invoke_signed with the PDA's signer seeds. A helpful test flow is: deploy the program, create a mint where the PDA is the mint authority, call your wrapper instruction with an amount, and verify the destination token account balance increased. Don't embed private keys; rely on PDAs derived from seeds plus a bump. A common misconception is to assume the token program needs the program id as owner — instead the token program must be the SPL token program id while the PDA acts as an on-chain authority. Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Token Wrapper Starter
Starter code structure

The starter provides process_instruction with accounts for token mint, destination, PDA mint authority, and token program. You will add PDA seeds, create mint_to, and call invoke_signed.

Student TODO
Define seeds (for example b"mint_authority_pda" and bump), create mint_to instruction, prepare account array in expected order, and call invoke_signed.
use solana_program::{
  account_info::{next_account_info, AccountInfo},
  entrypoint,
  entrypoint::ProgramResult,
  msg,
  program::{invoke, invoke_signed},
  pubkey::Pubkey,
};
use spl_token::{instruction as token_instruction, ID as TOKEN_PROGRAM_ID};

entrypoint!(process_instruction);

pub fn process_instruction(
  program_id: &Pubkey,
  accounts: &[AccountInfo],
  instruction_data: &[u8],
) -> ProgramResult {
  // Assume instruction_data contains the amount (u64)
  let amount = u64::from_le_bytes(instruction_data.try_into().unwrap());

  let account_info_iter = &mut accounts.iter();
  let token_mint_account = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
  let destination_token_account = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
  let pda_mint_authority = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;
  let token_program = next_account_info(account_info_iter)?;

  // --- YOUR CODE HERE ---
  // 1. Define PDA seeds (e.g., b"mint_authority_pda" plus bump).
  // 2. Create the `mint_to` instruction using `spl_token::instruction::mint_to`.
  // 3. Call `invoke_signed` with correct accounts and signer seeds.
  // --- END YOUR CODE ---

screens.title: Validating accounts before CPI
screens.narratorSegment: Security during CPI starts with rigorous validation. Before you hand accounts to a callee, perform a small sequence of checks. First, confirm the token program account equals the known SPL Token Program ID. Second, verify that accounts expected to be token accounts are actually owned by the token program by inspecting account. owner. Third, ensure writable accounts have the is_writable flag set if the callee will mutate them. Fourth, check is_signer where appropriate: if the callee expects a signer provided by the transaction, ensure that flag is set; if you expect to use invoke_signed, ensure the PDA is passed and seeds reconstruct it. A recommended process is: validate static invariants first, then compute expected PDAs and compare, then assemble the AccountInfo slice, and finally make the external call. This ordering reduces the window where untrusted code can manipulate your program's state. A common weak point is assuming the client supplied the correct destination account; always confirm recipient ownership or an agreed identifier. By following this sequence you minimize risk of funds being moved to a malicious account or state being corrupted. Ask yourself: which check, if omitted, would be most catastrophic for your program's invariants?

Validation Flow
1. Program IDs
Confirm the callee program account equals the expected program id (e.g., SPL token).
2. Ownership
Verify account.owner for token accounts and PDAs before trusting roles.
3. Flags
Check is_signer and is_writable to match callee expectations.
Process
  1. Validate static invariants and ownership.
  2. Derive expected PDAs and compare keys.
  3. Assemble AccountInfo in exact callee order.
  4. Call invoke or invoke_signed and handle errors explicitly.
Key Takeaway

Run the validation sequence before any external call to minimize attack surface.

Common Mistake

Trusting client-supplied accounts without checking owner and signature flags.

screens.title: Reentrancy and external call design
screens.narratorSegment: Even though Solana's runtime and transaction model differ from traditional smart contract platforms, you should still design CPI flows to reduce reentrancy-like risks. A practical rule is to finalize internal state changes before making external calls or to structure state so that external calls cannot observe and exploit intermediate states. For example, if your program holds escrow state, mark the escrow as closed or update internal flags before calling out to another program to transfer funds. Alternatively, use a two-step approach: a validation and a commit step where the commit cannot be replayed without new signer proofs. Another helpful pattern is to minimize the amount of mutable state passed to the callee. If a callee can call back into your program during CPI, ensure your program's entry points validate preconditions and that important invariants cannot be violated mid-call. A common misconception is thinking reentrancy is impossible on Solana. While the execution model reduces some reentrancy vectors, malicious callee programs or unexpected CPIs can still create complex control flows. The pragmatic question to ask when designing a CPI is: if the callee were malicious, what sequence of calls could it use to change my program's state, and how can I eliminate or guard against that sequence?

  • Use commit/validation two-step flows to prevent replay of critical operations.

Scenario
An escrow program should mark an escrow as settled before invoking a token transfer to avoid a callback that attempts to reuse the same escrow.

screens.title: Testing CPI and PDAs end-to-end
screens.narratorSegment: Testing CPI flows requires end-to-end checks that exercise PDAs, signer seeds, and account ordering. Start by deriving the PDA in your test harness using the same seeds and bump your program uses; create a mint whose mint authority is that PDA. Next, set up destination token accounts and prepare the instruction_data your wrapper expects. Call the wrapper program via a local test transaction and assert that the destination account balance increases by the minted amount. Also include negative tests: call with incorrect seeds, misordered accounts, or wrong token program id and confirm the call fails as expected. These failures are valuable: they prove your program correctly enforces expectations. When debugging, highlight the account_infos array you send and ensure its order matches the callee documentation. A common oversight is not testing the case where the PDA derivation changes due to a bump mismatch. Always include bump edge cases. After passing tests locally, follow your deployment checklist: deploy program, create on-chain mint with PDA as authority, and run the integration test against a devnet-like environment to verify the real runtime behavior. Testing CPI and PDAs end-to-end means create end-to-end tests that verify successful cpi behavior and failure modes like wrong seeds, misordered accounts, or incorrect program ids.. In practical terms, deploy, create mint with pda authority, and verify behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Test plan
Positive test
Derive PDA with seeds, create mint with PDA authority, call wrapper to mint, assert destination balance increased.
Negative tests
Use wrong seeds, wrong account order, or an incorrect token program id and assert calls fail as expected.
Debug tip
Print or log the account public keys and derived PDA in tests to confirm the expected ordering and derivation match runtime expectations.

Integration tests that cover both success and failure modes give you confidence in CPI logic and safety checks.

screens.title: Common errors and how to diagnose them
screens.narratorSegment: When a CPI fails at runtime, the most frequent causes are misordered accounts, incorrect program id for the callee, or missing signer authority for a PDA. Start debugging by checking the error the runtime returned. If it signals invalid account data or incorrect program id, confirm the token program account you passed equals the expected SPL Token Program ID. If the callee complains about missing signer, ensure you passed the PDA and supplied invoke_signed with correct seeds. To diagnose account ordering, print the account public keys and map them to the callee's expected positions in code or tests; compare that mapping to the callee’s documentation. If the data layout is unexpected, verify the owner fields and inspect the account data length and layout if possible. Another helpful approach is to write focused unit tests that intentionally swap two accounts to confirm the failure mode and isolate which position the callee expects for each role. Remember that the callee executes its own validation and will reject malformed inputs; thus careful pre-call validation and well-structured tests will greatly speed troubleshooting. Close by asking: which diagnostic step will you run first when you see an invalid account error?

  1. Confirm the callee program id equals expected program (e.g., SPL token).
  2. Verify signer errors: did you use invoke_signed with correct seeds?

Methodical checks and targeted tests that alter account order are the fastest route to identify CPI failures.

fullNarratorScript:
Cross-Program Invocation, or CPI, is the mechanism Solana uses to let one deployed program request work from another program. CPI enables composability: your program can rely on a shared token program for transfers, or call a lending program to update state, rather than reimplementing that logic. In practice CPI means assembling the exact instruction the callee expects, collecting the required AccountInfo objects in the correct order, and deciding whether the calling program must supply a signature. That decision determines whether you use invoke or invoke_signed. A concrete example you will see in this chapter is an escrow program delegating an SPL Token transfer. The escrow does not implement token logic; it calls the SPL Token Program and, if the escrow owns the source account, it uses invoke_signed and signer seeds so the program can sign for a Program Derived Address. We will also cover defensive practices: verifying ownership, writable flags, and signer expectations, and how misordered accounts commonly cause runtime failures. By the end of this chapter you will be able to assemble CPI calls, choose the appropriate invoke function, supply signer seeds for PDAs, and validate accounts before making external calls. Consider: what checks would you perform first before handing an external program access to your accounts?

Over the next screens you will develop four specific skills that let your Solana program operate safely and collaboratively with other programs. First, you will understand the purpose and mechanics of Cross-Program Invocation so you can reason about when a program should call another rather than duplicating logic. For example, a trading program may call the SPL Token Program to move tokens instead of writing token code from scratch. Second, you will learn to construct CPI calls using invoke and invoke_signed. That includes assembling the instruction, collecting AccountInfo objects and choosing whether to provide signer seeds. Third, you will identify why account ordering and signer requirements are critical; we'll drill into how swapping two accounts will cause the callee to misinterpret roles and often fail. Finally, you will implement a practical example where a program invokes SPL Token instructions and uses signer seeds for a PDA. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or milestone to help you track competency. By the end you’ll be able to validate accounts before CPI and reason about safety implications. Which of these will matter most when you deploy a wrapper that mints tokens for users?

This second objectives screen focuses on how you will apply the skills and what mastery looks like. Applying CPI means writing code that constructs an instruction for a callee, collects AccountInfo objects in the callee-expected order, and chooses invoke or invoke_signed based on whether a program-controlled PDA must sign. A practical application is a wrapper program that mints tokens by calling the SPL Token Program: you will derive a PDA, make it the mint authority, construct a mint_to instruction that lists the mint, destination, authority, and token program in the order expected, and call invoke_signed with the PDA's signer seeds. Mastery means you can both implement the CPI and write tests that deploy a mint with your PDA as authority, call your wrapper instruction, and confirm account balances changed as expected. You will also be able to reason about and prevent security pitfalls: validate account. owner matches expected programs, check is_signer and is_writable flags, and protect state from adverse reentrancy. The milestone here is a passing end-to-end test that mints tokens using your PDA under controlled checks.

Cross-Program Invocation is the mechanism that lets one Solana program ask another deployed program to execute an instruction on its behalf. Put simply, CPI turns programs into modular services: instead of reimplementing token transfer logic you call the SPL Token Program. A clear definition helps you reason about authority, ownership, and the limits of each program's control. The callee receives a prepared instruction and an ordered slice of AccountInfo objects describing which accounts to read or modify, and it enforces its own validation rules. A useful mental model is: the invoker composes an instruction packet and offers it to a callee that already knows how to act on those accounts. A concrete example is an escrow program that needs to transfer tokens: the escrow builds the token transfer instruction that the SPL Token Program understands, supplies the source account, destination account, authority account, and token program account, and calls invoke_signed if the escrow must sign via a PDA. A common misconception is thinking CPI magically shares signer authority; it does not. The invoking program only gains signing power for a derived PDA when it supplies correct signer seeds to invoke_signed. As you learn CPI, keep that model in mind: instruction packet, account ordering, and explicit signing are the three pillars.

In Solana, accounts are described to the callee as a slice of AccountInfo objects. Each AccountInfo contains metadata: the public key, the owner program, whether the account signed the original transaction, whether it is writable, and a pointer to its data. When you prepare a CPI you must assemble each AccountInfo the callee expects and pass them in the exact order the callee's instruction parser assumes. Practically, that means you cannot rely on position-agnostic lookup — the callee binds roles to positions: account 0 might be the source token account, account 1 the destination, account 2 the authority, and so on. A concrete scenario is the SPL Token transfer instruction: it expects source, destination, authority (and the token program account in some cases). If you swap those positions the SPL Token Program will read the wrong account as the authority and the instruction will fail validation. Another important detail is the distinction between account. owner and program-derived ownership: you must verify that an account that must be owned by a particular program actually is, and that a PDA you expect to sign is derived from your program id and known seeds. A common rookie error is trusting the client-supplied accounts without checking owner and signer flags. Always perform those checks before constructing and issuing a CPI.

Solana exposes two primary runtime helpers for CPI: invoke and invoke_signed. invoke is used when the invoking program does not need to sign for any accounts in the callee instruction. In such cases the required signatures are already present on the transaction, usually because the end user signed, and the invoker simply relays the instruction. A concrete example is a proxy program that forwards a user-signed delegation instruction to the SPL Token Program. invoke_signed is required when the invoking program must sign for a Program Derived Address it controls. With invoke_signed you supply signer seeds: byte arrays used by the runtime to reconstruct the PDA and allow the program to sign on its behalf. This enables common patterns like a program-owned escrow or a wrapper program that mints tokens where the mint authority is a PDA. A frequent misconception is believing that invoke_signed automatically signs any account; it only signs PDAs derived from your program id using the seeds you supply. Also be aware that the signer seeds must exactly reconstruct the PDA and that all PDA signer accounts passed to the callee must be in the expected positions. The practical rule is: if any account in the callee instruction requires a signature that your program must provide, use invoke_signed with the correct seeds; otherwise invoke suffices.

Program Derived Addresses, or PDAs, are public keys derived deterministically from seeds and a program id. They allow a program to have accounts it effectively controls without a private key. To use a PDA as a signer during CPI, you must call invoke_signed with the exact set of seeds used to derive that PDA. The runtime reconstructs the PDA from seeds and program id, verifies the PDA, and if it matches the supplied account the runtime treats it as signed by the program. A practical pattern: when a program owns a token account, that account is often owned by the program via a PDA authority. To transfer from that account you must supply the PDA as the authority and call invoke_signed with the original seeds. A common pitfall is using seeds that do not exactly match the derivation: even a single byte difference prevents the runtime from recognizing the PDA and the callee will reject the missing signature. Another mistake is forgetting to include the PDA account in the AccountInfo slice passed to the callee or placing it in the wrong position. When designing seeds, choose stable domain-like seeds such as a descriptive string plus a bump. Document the seeds, use a deterministic bump, and always check the PDA owner before relying on it as an authority.

Let's walk through a concise token transfer pattern where a program-owned PDA signs an SPL Token transfer using invoke_signed. The invoker prepares the SPL Token transfer instruction with the source token account, destination token account, and authority set to the PDA. It then constructs the AccountInfo slice in the exact order the SPL Token Program expects. Next, the program provides signer seeds that reconstruct the PDA, wrapped as an array of seed slices, and calls invoke_signed. In practice you should first validate that the token program account matches the SPL Token Program ID, that the source and destination are proper token accounts owned by the token program, and that the PDA is derived from your program id using the expected seeds. A misconception to avoid is trusting the provided authority account without derivation checks; instead compute the expected PDA locally and compare the public key. For a concrete example, the escrow pattern passes source, destination, pda_authority, and token_program in that order and uses a seeds array such as [b"escrow", bump]. After invoke_signed completes, check the result and update any on-chain escrow state. As a closing question: how would you structure your checks so that no external call happens until all invariants are validated?

This hands-on starter demonstrates the wrapper program pattern: your program will call the SPL Token Program's mint_to instruction using invoke_signed so a PDA acts as mint authority. The starter structure provides a process_instruction entrypoint that expects accounts for the token mint, destination token account, PDA mint authority, and the token program account. Your task is to define the PDA seeds, construct the mint_to instruction passing the PDA as authority, prepare the AccountInfo slice in the order the SPL Token Program expects, and call invoke_signed with the PDA's signer seeds. When a CPI fails at runtime, the most frequent causes are misordered accounts, incorrect program id for the callee, or missing signer authority for a PDA. Start debugging by checking the error the runtime returned. If it signals invalid account data or incorrect program id, confirm the token program account you passed equals the expected SPL Token Program ID. If the callee complains about missing signer, ensure you passed the PDA and supplied invoke_signed with correct seeds. To diagnose account ordering, print the account public keys and map them to the callee's expected positions in code or tests; compare that mapping to the callee’s documentation. If the data layout is unexpected, verify the owner fields and inspect the account data length and layout if possible. Let's summarize the core ideas you must carry forward. Cross-Program Invocation is the mechanism to call another program's instruction so functionality can be composed without duplication. The invoke helper is used when your program does not need to sign for any accounts; it relays instructions where required signatures are already present. The invoke_signed helper must be used when a program needs to act as the signer for a Program Derived Address: you provide the signer seeds and the runtime reconstructs the PDA to allow the program to sign. Keep these three concepts distinct in your mental model. A strong habit is to write down the account order expected by the callee and validate each AccountInfo before invoking.
